title: 037 Tagging an Image

segments.text: At this point, we have the ability to create a new custom image out of our Docker file, and we can do so by running Docker Build.
The output from all that is this very last line right here that says successfully built blah blah blah.
This is the ID of the image that was just created, so we can now create a container out of this image by copying the ID and running Docker run and then placing the ID in there.
Now, when we run this command, an instance of our image we created will get a new container, and inside that we're going to be running an instance of rediscover.
So I'll hit enter, and there we go. We've got our copy of redis, and again, all the warnings you can totally ignore.
Now, one thing I want to point out here is that having to execute Docker run and then paste in that ID, I don't have any more, but having to paste in that ID is kind of a pain.
And as sure was a lot nicer earlier in the course, when we were able to do stuff like just simply Docker run redis or Docker run hello world.
In those cases, we didn't have to memorize an ID to use. So we can actually do the same by slightly changing the form of the Docker build command.
Here's what we're going to do. We are going to run Docker build, and then we're going to add on this little argument right here that is going to tag the image that is created.
And make it a lot easier to refer to it by a name that you and I can customize.

The convention for this is your Docker ID, a slash, the name of the project that you're working on, a colon, and then the version, which traditionally is going to be latest whenever you're building the newest version of an image.
But in general, that is supposed to actually be a version. So traditionally a number or for the latest version of your image, you simply say latest.
Now, this is a convention right here. You're going to see all projects in Docker trying to follow this convention as much as possible.
You might be wondering why some other images that we've been able to use have more simplified names like simply redis or hello dash world or busy box.
Well, all those are community images. They're images that have been created by people in the community and kind of open source for very popular use.
Any time that you are creating an image of your own, you're always going to prefix it with your Docker ID.
All right. So let's give this a shot and see how it works. So I'm going to flip back or my terminal.
And we are going to execute Docker build dash t your Docker ID. So for me, it's even greater for you. It's probably going to be something else slash whatever you want the name of the project to be.
So I'm going to use redis. You can do redis. You can do redis server really anything goes here.
A colon and I'll say specifically latest and then don't forget after all that stuff, we still have to put in that dot at the very end.
Still need to specify that build context, which again is the source of all the files and folders that are going to be used to build your container out.
One quick reminder, we're not really doing a lot with this build context yet, but we will use it for something later on in the course.
All right. So once you got all that in there, we'll run that and then the output down here says successfully built the image ID, but then it tagged it as this name.
And so now we can start up a container out of this image by running Docker run and then using the name that we just provided of Steven Grider or whatever your tag is slash redis.
And then you do not have to actually specify the version on the end, you can simply leave it as your doc or idea slash redis.
If you don't put on the version on the end, then the latest version of the container or they see me the latest version of the image will be used by default.
So I'll run that and sure enough we get our Docker image running.
All right. So one last quick kind of nitpick thing that I want to throw out here just because you might see some documentation looks a little bit confusing.
Technically, the version number on the very end tier, this is technically the tag.
Now the entire process of what we just did is known as tagging the image and even the argument we used was dash to you right here.
So we call this process tag in the image, but technically just the version on the end is the tag.
Everything else on here is actually like the repository or the project name. So just a little bit of a nitpick. I just want you to be aware of that.
All right. So that's pretty much it. Let's take a quick break and we'll continue in the next section.
